Yet he concealed one secret from these cherished friends, a secret he had fostered since his earliest childhood. Though he loved his companions at college, he would not entrust it to the sympathy or discretion of any among them. He was in love. He feared they might mock the ardour of his feeling, and could not endure their profaning it by treating as slight and fleeting what he knew to be the very life within his life.

Near his family’s mansion lived a gentleman of modest means with three lovely daughters. The eldest was by far the fairest, yet her beauty merely supplemented her other virtues: her mind was lucid and vigorous, her temper angelically mild. She and my father had played together from infancy. Even as a child, Diana had been a favourite of his mother, whose fondness increased as the beautiful, spirited girl grew older; thus they were constantly together throughout his school and college holidays. Novels, and all the other means through which civilized youth learn of passions before actually experiencing them, had powerfully influenced one so unusually open to impressions. At eleven, Diana was his favourite companion in play, but already he spoke the language of a lover. She was nearly two years older than he, yet her upbringing had left her more childlike, at least in understanding and expressing emotion. Innocently she accepted his ardent declarations and returned them without knowing their meaning. She had read no novels and kept company only with her younger sisters; how could she distinguish love from friendship? By the time her developing intelligence revealed the true character of their relationship, her heart already belonged to her friend. Her only fear was that new attractions or inconstancy might lead him to abandon his childhood promises.

Instead, those promises grew more tender and impassioned each day. His love had developed alongside him, entwining itself with every power and feeling of his being, and could end only with his life. Their two hearts alone knew their secret. Though in this, as in every other matter, he feared his companions’ criticism—feared their judging him for sincerely loving someone poorer than himself—nothing ever shook, even for an instant, his resolve to marry her once he found the courage to confront the obstacles he meant to overcome.

Diana was entirely deserving of his most profound affection.

Uttering these cries, many of the women, driven into unseeing fury, spun about and struck and clawed at their own companions until they sank in an impassioned faint. Only the men who belonged to them prevented their being trampled.

Yet not an instant was wasted—not an instant! This Foulon was at the Hotel de Ville and might be released. Never, if Saint Antoine remembered his own misery, humiliation, and wrongs! Armed women and men poured from the Quarter so swiftly, drawing even these last remnants along in so powerful a current, that in fifteen minutes not a living soul remained within Saint Antoine except a few ancient women and the crying children.

No. By then they were all crowding the Hall of Examination, where the wicked, ugly old man stood, and spilling out into the adjoining square and streets. Husband and wife Defarge, The Vengeance, and Jacques Three were at the front of the crush, not far from him inside the Hall.

“Look!” shouted madame, indicating him with her knife. “Look at the old scoundrel tied up in ropes! A fine thing, fastening that bundle of grass on his back. Ha, ha! Very well done. Let him eat it now!” She tucked her knife beneath her arm and applauded as though watching a play.

The people immediately behind Madame Defarge told those behind them what pleased her, and those passed it to others, who passed it to others still, until the nearby streets echoed with applause. Likewise, throughout two or three hours of tedious speech and the sifting of countless bushels of words, her frequent signs of impatience were repeated far away with astonishing speed. This was easier because certain men, who had climbed the building’s exterior with extraordinary agility to peer through the windows, knew Madame Defarge well and served as a telegraph between her and the crowd outside.

At last the sun climbed high enough to send a kindly beam, suggestive of hope or shelter, directly upon the old captive’s head. That favour was intolerable. In a moment the barrier of dust and chaff, which had endured surprisingly long, scattered to the wind, and Saint Antoine had seized him!

The news instantly reached the crowd’s most distant edges. Defarge had only just leaped a railing and table to clasp the wretched man in a fatal embrace; Madame Defarge had only just followed and wound her hand into one of his binding ropes; The Vengeance and Jacques Three had not yet reached them, nor had the men at the windows swooped from their lofty stations into the Hall like hunting birds, when the cry seemed to rise across the entire city: “Bring him out!

Eventually we agreed to live together for the duration of my stay in the city. Since my finances were somewhat less strained than his, he allowed me to pay for renting and furnishing a strange, decaying mansion. We furnished it to suit the rather fanciful gloom we shared. Long abandoned because of superstitions we never investigated, it stood close to collapse in a secluded, desolate part of the Faubourg St. Germain.

Had the world known our daily routine there, it would have considered us mad, though perhaps harmlessly so. Our isolation was complete. We received no visitors. In fact, I carefully concealed the location from my former acquaintances, and many years had passed since Dupin had known anyone, or been known, in Paris. We lived entirely within our own world.

My friend had a peculiar fancy—what else can I call it?—for loving night simply for itself. I quietly adopted this eccentricity as I did all his others, surrendering myself completely to his extravagant whims. The dark goddess could not remain with us forever, but we could imitate her presence. At the first light of dawn we shut all the old building’s untidy shutters and lit two heavily scented candles. These gave off only the faintest, most ghostly light. By their glow we occupied our minds with dreams, reading, writing, or talking until the clock announced the arrival of actual darkness. Then we ventured into the streets arm in arm, continuing our earlier discussions or wandering far and wide until late. Among the crowded city’s vivid lights and shadows, we sought the endless stimulation that quiet observation can provide.

During these walks I could not help noticing and admiring Dupin’s unusual analytical talent, although his rich imagination had prepared me to expect something of the kind. He also seemed to take intense pleasure in using this ability, if not precisely in showing it off, and readily admitted how much he enjoyed it. With a low chuckle, he boasted that, as far as he was concerned, most men had windows in their chests. He often followed such claims with startling, direct evidence of how thoroughly he understood my own heart. At these moments his manner became cold and distant, and his eyes looked blank. His voice, normally a full tenor, climbed into a high register that would have sounded peevish had he not spoken with such deliberate care and absolute clarity.
